description: We are BrydanWorld, a young and curious team led by 9-year-old Nivaan from India. We love space exploration, robotics, coding, and creative problem-solving. With experience in Scratch, Python, and beginner electronics projects, we aim to make space science fun through interactive games and simulations. Our mission is to learn, experiment, and build something meaningful for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We welcome creative minds interested in space, science, game design, and coding!
summary:
HORIZON is an interactive lunar mission training game developed by Team BrydanWorld for young learners. It transforms complex space engineering challenges into an engaging, decision-based learning experience.

Players become mission commanders responsible for protecting four astronauts at a lunar south pole outpost during a seven-day mission. Each day presents a new challenge involving power generation, oxygen supply, water management, food production, radiation protection, or crew safety.

Players must choose between competing solutions, each with benefits and consequences. For example, reducing greenhouse lighting can conserve electricity but slow food production. Their decisions change the outpost's resources and influence whether the mission succeeds or fails.

HORIZON uses simplified educational simulations informed by publicly available NASA research on life-support systems, plant growth in space, and radiation protection. Its resource values are illustrative rather than actual NASA mission measurements.

Our goal is to make space science accessible, interactive, and meaningful while encouraging children to think critically, solve problems, and understand real engineering trade-offs.
details:
HORIZON — Junior Lunar Mission Trainer

The Problem

Space exploration requires engineers to balance limited resources while keeping astronauts safe. However, these complex engineering decisions are often difficult for young learners to understand through textbooks or traditional quizzes.

Our Solution

HORIZON is an interactive, browser-based lunar mission training game designed to help students experience the challenges of managing a Moon base.

Players take the role of Mission Commander, responsible for protecting four astronauts during a seven-day mission at a simulated lunar south pole outpost.

How It Works

Each mission day introduces an engineering challenge involving essential lunar base systems, including:

  • Power generation and battery management
  • Oxygen supply and life-support systems
  • Water conservation
  • Food production and greenhouse operations
  • Radiation protection
  • Crew health and safety

Players evaluate three possible responses to each challenge. Every option involves trade-offs: improving one resource may reduce another.

For example, reducing greenhouse lighting saves electricity but slows food production. Prioritizing scientific research may consume resources needed for crew survival.

The game updates resource indicators after each decision and explains the scientific reasoning behind the consequences.

Players succeed by maintaining critical resources and crew health throughout the seven-day mission. Poor decisions can lead to mission failure.

Technology Used

HORIZON was developed as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The game includes interactive decision-making, resource tracking, mission feedback, educational explanations, and a downloadable mission report. It is designed to run without a backend server or external gameplay services.

Scientific Foundation

The educational concepts were informed by publicly available NASA resources covering environmental control and life-support systems, plant growth in space, radiation protection, and lunar environmental challenges.

The game's resource values and decision outcomes are simplified educational models. They are not actual NASA engineering measurements, operational predictions, or NASA-validated calculations.

What Makes HORIZON Unique?

Rather than asking students to memorize facts, HORIZON encourages them to make engineering decisions and observe their consequences.

It combines storytelling, resource management, scientific explanations, and mission-based learning in an accessible experience designed for children.

Educational Impact

HORIZON aims to develop critical thinking, systems thinking, scientific curiosity, and problem-solving skills.

Students learn that successful space missions depend not on maximizing a single resource, but on balancing interconnected systems and making responsible decisions under constraints.

Project Status

HORIZON is a completed, playable educational prototype featuring a seven-day lunar mission, interactive decisions, resource tracking, learning explanations, and a final mission report.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Development Transparency

Team BrydanWorld used ChatGPT (OpenAI) as an AI-assisted development tool during the creation of HORIZON. AI assistance was used for brainstorming, HTML, CSS and JavaScript code generation, debugging, user interface design, and drafting educational content and project documentation.

The team guided the project's development, selected its features and learning objectives, and worked on integrating the interactive lunar mission experience.

HORIZON does not use artificial intelligence during gameplay. Its decisions, resource calculations, and mission outcomes are implemented through predefined JavaScript logic.

The scientific concepts are informed by publicly available NASA educational resources. All resource values and simulated outcomes are simplified for educational purposes and are not official NASA mission calculations.
